request.lesson: A shipped-instruction check keyed on a fixed N-line window around a statement is satisfiable by adding lines rather than by fixing the defect. Two explanatory comment lines pushed a statement's governing transition out of a six-line window, turning a flagging check green while the property went unverified. Key such a check on an enclosing structural boundary such as a fenced block, and assert a non-vacuity floor naming how many sites must have been examined.

A plan that specifies more test mechanism than an implementer needs generates its own review findings. Across five spec-stage review rounds on install-to-ship-walkthrough the counts fell 26, 10, 8, 4, 1, but 6 of the 10 in round 2 and 6 of the 8 in round 3 were defects introduced by the previous round's repairs, not by the original draft. Each of those rounds converged only when the repair REMOVED a claim: a two-altitude source-plus-rendered check design collapsed to rendered-only, a browser-gate visibility claim was withdrawn to a stated accepted gap, and a scalar route count became a committed route set. new-spec already names this rule -- when a reviewer keeps finding under-specification in the plan rather than defects in the spec, the plan is over-specified: reduce it, do not extend it. Treat a review round whose findings are majority prior-round-repair as the signal to cut, and mark every finding draft-origin or prior-round-repair so the ratio is visible. The follow-on slice was then drafted at 4 criteria and 3 tasks rather than 14 and 5.

Late semantic review is the wrong place to discover deterministic repository obligations. In a six-case paired review experiment, 22 of 67 sustained findings were unmet repository conventions, split 11/11 between baseline and candidate. Projection drift affected five of six cases; register or backlog contradictions, release version and changelog obligations, approval-pinned deviations, eval coverage, and non-failing controls made up the rest. Because the cost was symmetric and repairs repeated the same breaches, changing review scheduling cannot remove it. Carry touched-path ground rules into the implementer brief, verify deterministic obligations before review, and retain focused re-review as a backstop for repair-induced defects.

Applying a sustained review finding to the surface the finding cites leaves the sibling surfaces that carry the same obligation contradicting it. One obligation lives in up to five places: the acceptance criterion, its verification group, and the plan's Tests, Approach and stub-disposition Constraint. Repairing only the cited one produced two confirmed regressions in one round — a task whose test bullets required descriptor-anchored traversal while its pinned stub Constraint still said 'canonicalise before opening', and an absent-input case removed from a criterion but left in the plan's pinned lifecycle test. spec-authoring-rubric.md's 'Find the property's siblings' names this class exactly, but work-loop's FIX section compresses it to 'fix the established defect, not the symptom' and routes nowhere, so an agent applying findings from FIX rather than through new-spec step 7 has the idea without the checklist or the mechanical check.

Re-verified 2026-09-17. The instance this lesson was drawn from is now repaired in code, and the repair's own comment records the history that produced the lesson. A principle whose worked example has been fixed does not stop being true, but the record has to say which half is history, or a reader checks the cited code, finds the guard present, and concludes the whole lesson is stale.

A byte digest pinned to a file the lesson is not about goes stale on the first unrelated edit and says nothing when it does. Dropped .github/workflows/build-check.yml from this topic's supporting sources: the claim is about a technique, not about those bytes, and the pin had already drifted while the lesson stayed true. Pin a source only when the claim is about its contents.

A criterion that asserts a table is total 'over the inputs it names' takes its domain from the artifact under test, so an omitted or renamed row redefines the property instead of failing it. Two separate defects in one delivery came from that shape: a routing table was total over its own three row keys while two of the six consequences in the firing predicate beside it matched no row at all, and an evidence-shape table's key set was checked against itself. The repair is two-part and neither half works alone. Write the control's expected key set as a literal fixture in the test and compare the parsed keys against it before building any mapping, so a renamed or missing row fails. And make the table total by construction rather than by a second enumeration: one row is the residual route defined as 'any of the above unless a row below applies', and the exception rows are made mutually exclusive on a single stated discriminator. A second enumeration of a domain is a second home for it and is free to drift from the first, which is how the two unmapped consequences arose.

A delivery brief's Success metrics section drifts below brief altitude when it is patched round after round. Answering a shaping reviewer's 'one-sided contract' finding by adding criteria makes the section grow, and each addition contradicts scope or non-goals somewhere else, so the next round finds more. The tell that it has gone too far is a finding that asks for a checker name, an exit code, or a read boundary: that is spec-owned detail, so the section is no longer at brief altitude. Rebuild the section as a handful of outcome-level observations that bind in both directions, and state explicitly that falsifiable criteria are spec-owned. Patching it again does not converge. A second, related trap: repairing only the section a finding names leaves the same defect in every other section the rule touches, so a fixed count removed from Non-goals can survive in Post-Ready decisions and return as a later finding. Sweep every occurrence, not the named one.
